resources.string: No estimates yet. PacingLab estimates VO2max from runs with steady stretches, and adds the values Fitbit writes after GPS runs.
Add a lab or field test
A measured VO2max, for example from a lab test with gas analysis. It counts more than any estimate.

VO2max, the most oxygen your body can use, in ml per kg per minute. The line is PacingLab's best estimate of your true value over time, the band one standard deviation of its uncertainty.

# Where the values come from
- Test (diamond): a lab or field test you entered. The most trusted value.
- Fitbit (filled dot): the estimate Fitbit writes to Health Connect after some GPS runs. With the Google Health API connected, Fitbit's daily cardio fitness series adds its runs from before it wrote to Health Connect and says how much Fitbit trusted each one: its daily value is Fitbit's own Kalman filter, and undoing each update gives back the run measurement and its noise. A run Fitbit itself passed over is left out, and the more Fitbit trusted a run, the more it counts.
- PacingLab (hollow dot): estimated from every run with steady stretches, interval reps included. Runs without a speed recording use their GPS track.

# PacingLab's estimate
- Steady stretches: four minutes of even pace whose heart rate has levelled off. Heart rate needs about three minutes to settle, so short warm-ups give no estimate.
- The oxygen cost of the pace by the ACSM running equation, on the flat.
- The share of your heart rate reserve used equals the share of your VO2 reserve (Swain and Leutholtz 1997), which gives VO2max from the cost.
- It depends on correct maximum and resting heart rate and assumes average running economy.

# The trend
A Kalman filter treats your true VO2max as changing slowly, about 1 ml/kg/min a month, and every value as a noisy measurement of it. Each source's noise is learned from how much it scatters around the trend, so steadier sources pull the line harder. A smoother then uses later values too, for the best picture of the past.

The number at the top is today's value from the estimates so far; its uncertainty grows on days without new ones.

# Heat
Heat raises heart rate at a given pace, so a warm run underestimates VO2max. Each of PacingLab's run estimates is adjusted to cool conditions with the weather at the run: across 1,258 elite races performance fell by 0.3 to 0.4 % per degree of WBGT above 15 °C (Mantzios 2022), so the oxygen cost above rest is raised by 0.35 % per degree. The races were run all out; for steady running this is an assumption, and it matches heart rate running a few beats higher on warm days. Fitbit's values and tests are left as they are. Needs Settings > Data > Weather for sessions.

# Fitness age
The age at which your VO2max is the average of healthy people of your sex in the HUNT3 Fitness Study (4,600 Norwegians, measured on a treadmill; Loe 2013), as NTNU's Cardiac Exercise Research Group defines it. The averages per decade are joined by straight lines; 20 is the youngest age shown. VO2max is one of the strongest predictors of mortality (Kodama 2009: about 13 % lower risk for every 3.5 ml/kg/min), which is what makes the comparison worth showing. Set your birth date in Settings to see the average for your age.
Pace at %1$d bpm in each run with steady easy running, and its six-week average

How fast you run at an easy heart rate, here %1$d bpm (85 %% of your threshold). As aerobic fitness grows, the same heart rate carries you faster.

# How it is measured
- Only steady stretches count: two minutes of even pace with heart rate levelled off, at 80 to 90 %% of threshold heart rate.
- Each run gives speed per heartbeat over those stretches (the efficiency factor of endurance coaching), turned into the pace it means at %1$d bpm.
- The line is the average of the last six weeks of runs.

# When it appears
It needs at least three steady minutes at an easy heart rate in a run. Short warm-ups, where heart rate is still climbing, and interval sessions do not count, so zone 2 runs fill it.

# Limits
Heat, hills, wind and fatigue slow a single run; compare the line, not single dots.

# Heat
On warm runs (WBGT above 15 °C) the pace is raised by 0.35 %% per degree to stand for cool conditions (Mantzios 2022), since heat lifts heart rate at a given pace. The line under the chart counts the runs this applied to.
Includes watch speed without GPS: an estimate

- VO2max: the Daniels and Gilbert (1979) equations behind Daniels' VDOT tables. The predicted time is the pace whose oxygen cost matches the share of VO2max that can be held that long. It uses today's value from the VO2max card.
- Critical speed: (distance − D′) / CS, only for races of 2 to 30 minutes, where the model holds.

# Limits
Both assume an all-out race and training suited to the distance. PacingLab's VO2max partly rests on watch estimates. Read them as what your fitness allows, not as a promise.

# Marathon shape
A marathon needs long runs and weekly distance that a VO2max value cannot show, so the VO2max times of long races are tempered by Runalyze's marathon shape:
- Weekly distance over the last six months (at least 70 days) against VO2max^1.135 km, two thirds of the shape.
- Runs over 13 km in the last ten weeks, each worth ((km − 13) / (target − 13))², the target being 12 ln(VO2max / 4) km, weighted from 2 for today down to 0 after 70 days; one target long run a week fills this third.
- A race over d km asks for a shape of d^1.23 %: about 7 % for 5 km, 43 % for a half and 100 % for a marathon. Short of it, the race is run at a smaller share of VO2max, down to 60 %.

Runalyze says itself that this is a heuristic from typical marathon plans, not a validated model. The time below a tempered one is what VO2max alone predicts.

# What it is
Critical speed (CS) is the highest speed at which fatigue does not build up steadily. Above it you can run only a fixed distance, D′, before you must slow down. It lies close to threshold pace.

# How it is found
From your training, as in Smyth and Muniz-Pumares (2020): the farthest distance in 3, 7 and 12 minutes over the last 12 weeks, fitted with distance = CS × time + D′. Only sustained efforts count: no slowing to recover, and heart rate at threshold in their second half. The best 12 minutes of an interval session include recoveries and would make CS far too slow.

# Getting a value
Run 3 minutes and 12 minutes all out with GPS (Run mode, not Interval mode), on separate days or with 30 minutes of easy jogging between. A 7-minute effort makes the fit sturdier.

Best pace for %1$d durations from one minute up

resources.string:
The fastest time over each distance and the farthest distance in each duration, found anywhere in your runs, not only in races.

# Two sources
- GPS: the track of runs recorded with GPS.
- Watch, no GPS: the watch's own speed from steps and stride length, used for interval workouts, which the Sense records without GPS. Nothing can check it, and at the same heart rate it read about 14 % faster than GPS in your runs, so it is drawn dashed and grey and set in italics. Sprint workouts are left out: at sprint speed the watch reads far too fast.

# Cleaning
A stretch counts only if heart rate reached 75 % of your maximum by half a minute after it, which keeps out rides in a vehicle. GPS steps faster than 9 m/s count as a pause.

Decoupling of %1$d steady long runs against the 5 percent line

resources.string:
On a long steady run, heart rate drifts up at an unchanged pace once aerobic endurance runs short. Decoupling compares speed per heartbeat in the second half of the run with the first (Friel). Under 5 % counts as good aerobic endurance for that duration.

# Which runs count
Steady runs of at least 40 minutes: the first 10 minutes are left out as warm-up, and the rest needs few stops and an even pace. Interval sessions never count.

# Limits
Hills, heat and dehydration also raise heart rate.

# Heat
Heat makes heart rate drift more, so a warm run (WBGT 18 °C or more) decouples more without any loss of endurance. Its dot is hollow; compare it with other warm runs rather than with cool ones.

Reps of 3 to 5 minutes at VO2max
Short fast reps for speed and economy

Daniels' training intensities (Daniels' Running Formula), from today's VO2max on the VO2max card. Each is a share of VO2max turned into a pace with the Daniels-Gilbert oxygen cost of running, as in his VDOT tables:

- Easy: 59 to 74 % of VO2max. Most of the week's running.
- Marathon: the predicted marathon pace, without the marathon shape correction.
- Threshold: 88 %, about the pace you could race for an hour. Sessions of 20 minutes steady or reps of 5 to 15 minutes with short rests.
- Interval: 97.5 %, the pace you could race for 10 to 15 minutes. Reps of 3 to 5 minutes, recoveries a little shorter than the reps.
- Repetition: 105 %, about mile race pace. Reps of up to 2 minutes with full recoveries.

At VO2max 50 these give 4:31, 4:15, 3:55 and 3:42 per km, Daniels' published values. Heat, hills and wind slow every pace; on such days go by effort.
Drop in the minute after hard reps
Heart rate drop in the minute after hard reps, per interval session, with the median of five sessions

How far heart rate falls in the first minute after a hard rep, the standard measure of heart rate recovery (Cole 1999; review by Daanen 2012). It comes from the parasympathetic nervous system taking over again after effort: a faster drop comes with better aerobic fitness, and a slower one than usual with accumulated fatigue (Buchheit 2014).

# How it is measured
- Only reps whose peak heart rate reached 85 % of your maximum, followed by a recovery of at least a minute: harder reps fall further, so only hard ones are compared.
- The drop runs from the rep's peak (the wrist sensor lags, so up to 10 seconds after the rep) to the average of the 5 seconds a minute later.
- Each dot is a session: the median of its reps. The line is the median of the last five sessions.

# Why not after the session
Apple measures the drop in the minute after a workout ends. Sessions usually end with a cool-down or the way home, so heart rate after the stop says little and often rises. Reps within a session are a repeatable test instead.

Walked or jogged recoveries, heat and how fresh you are all move it, so read the line, not single dots.
